opus-5.5.text:
I think specialization is not only possible but probably inevitable, though maybe not in the clean way people imagine right now.

If you look at the history of computing, you eventually got a split between people building the general-purpose layer, like operating systems or foundation models, and people building applications on top. I do expect robotics to move in that direction. Training a really capable robot foundation model requires enormous amounts of diverse data, a lot of compute, and a research team that can iterate on architecture and training recipes. That's a very different muscle from going into a warehouse or a hospital or a kitchen and figuring out exactly what the customer needs, how the workflow runs, what the safety requirements are, how to get the unit economics to work.

But I'd push back a little on the idea that the split can happen cleanly today. Right now the models are not yet good enough that you can just hand one to an application company and say, "Here's the brain, go build your product." The boundary between the model and the deployment is still very blurry. When you deploy, you discover failure modes that tell you what data to collect, and that feeds back into the model. So at this stage, the companies that are closest to real deployments are generating a lot of the most valuable signal. If the brain company is too far from the field, it risks building something that looks impressive in demos but doesn't hold up in messy real environments.

So I think in the near term you'll see very tight partnerships, or vertically integrated players, where model developers work closely with a handful of deployment partners and the data loop is shared. Over time, as models become more general and more robust, and as interfaces like fine-tuning, evaluation, and data collection tooling mature, the layers can separate more. Then application companies can focus on their domain expertise, hardware choices, and customer relationships, while the foundation model companies focus on pushing general capability.

The other thing I'd say is that hardware complicates this compared with pure software AI. Robots have different embodiments, different sensors, different actuators. Part of the job of a good robot brain is to generalize across embodiments, and that's an active research problem. Until it's solved reasonably well, there's a lot of coupling between the brain and the body, and that also pushes toward closer collaboration rather than pure arm's-length specialization.

So my view is: long term, yes, a layered ecosystem similar to what we've seen in other technology waves. Short term, the most effective setups are ones where the people building the intelligence and the people deploying it in the real world are in very close contact, because that feedback loop is still where most of the progress comes from.

r001.rationale: The response describes application companies building on robot foundation models supplied by separate brain developers, and says that as the models mature, the layers can separate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the split is going to look a lot like what happened in computing, but it'll take longer to settle, and the boundary won't be where most people expect it right now.

The way I see it, a "robot brain" company is really building a foundation layer: a general model for perception, manipulation, and task planning that works across many different bodies and many different environments. That's enormously capital intensive. You need huge amounts of embodied data, you need the compute, and you need a team that can keep up with the frontier of the model research itself. Very few companies can sustain that, so I expect that layer to consolidate into a small number of players, and they'll make money by licensing or by running the model as a service.

The application companies are a different animal. If you're putting robots into a warehouse, or a hospital, or a restaurant kitchen, your core competence isn't the model. It's understanding the workflow, the regulations, the economics of that specific customer, and all the unglamorous stuff: integration, maintenance, uptime guarantees, training the staff who work alongside the machine. That knowledge is deep and local, and it doesn't transfer well from one vertical to another. So I think you'll see many application companies, each owning a vertical, rather than one giant that does everything.

Now, where it gets messy is the middle. The brain companies will be tempted to go vertical themselves, because the first one or two applications are where you prove the model works and where you collect the data that improves it. And the application companies will be tempted to build their own models, because they don't want to be dependent on someone else's roadmap and pricing. In the near term I think both of those things happen, and some of them will be painful experiments.

The thing that eventually forces specialization is data gravity and cost. Once a general brain is clearly better than anything a vertical player can build in-house, the economics push the application company to buy rather than build, the same way almost nobody builds their own cloud infrastructure today. But the brain companies will discover they can't service a thousand verticals themselves, and they'll need partners who actually understand the customer.

So my honest expectation: a lot of vertical integration for the next few years, and then a fairly sharp separation once the model layer matures. The interesting strategic question for anyone starting a company today is which side of that line you want to be standing on when the separation happens.

r001.rationale: The response says application companies will buy or license a general robot brain from specialized brain companies and apply it in specific verticals, describing the target business model.

astra-6.text:
I think there will be specialization, but the boundary won’t be clean at first. A company developing a robot brain still needs to deploy it in real applications to understand where it fails and get feedback. And a company commercializing robotics can’t simply plug in a brain and assume the problem is solved. It has to make the whole system reliable and economical for the customer.

Over time, I’d expect the brain companies to provide capabilities that work across different robots and tasks, while application companies build deep expertise in particular settings—factories, warehouses, or homes. Their value is in understanding the workflow, integrating the hardware, and delivering a service people will pay for.

The key is how those two sides learn together. If deployment experience feeds back into better models, specialization can work very well. If they operate in isolation, you can end up with an impressive model that doesn’t solve the customer’s problem.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes brain companies from application companies and says the latter integrate hardware, but it does not clearly state that application companies integrate robot brains supplied by other companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there will be specialization, but the boundary won’t be completely clean. A company developing the robot brain can focus on capabilities that transfer across tasks—perception, planning, and learning. An application company needs to understand a particular customer’s workflow: what the robot must do, how reliably it must do it, and whether the economics work.

The two sides need a close feedback loop. The brain company needs experience from real deployments, and the application company needs to influence how the capabilities develop. So early on, I’d expect more integration. As the technology and interfaces mature, there will be more room for specialized companies to work together.

r001.rationale: The response describes brain and application companies cooperating, but does not clearly state that application companies could integrate robot brains supplied by other companies.
